title.en: Five Days of Eclipse: The Torch of Katun 13 Ahau
title.zh: 五日蝕：十三阿赫卡特倫之火炬

texts.period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c.; Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. XI

texts.license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: The sky is set in its place by the first pope, the burden of Katun 13 Ahau — but the face of the sun shall be turned from its course and turned face down in the reign of the perishable rulers. For five days the sun is eclipsed, and then the torch of Katun 13 Ahau is seen: God's sign that death shall come to the rulers of the land and the first rulers driven from their towns.
summary.zh: 首任教皇——十三阿赫卡特倫之重負——將天空安置於其位；然而在朽壞統治者的朝代，日面將偏離其軌、翻身朝下。太陽蝕沒五日，其後十三阿赫卡特倫的火炬顯現：此乃上帝之兆，宣告死亡必臨此地統治者，最初的王將被逐出其城。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: Then the sky was put in its place, Corporales ti ojales, by the first pope, the face of the katun, the burden of the Katun 13 Ahau. The face of the sun shall be turned from its course, it shall be turned face down during the reign of the perishable men, the perishable rulers.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. XI; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Five days the sun is eclipsed, and then shall be seen the torch of Katun 13 Ahau, a sign given by God that death shall come to the rulers of this land. Thus it shall come about that the first rulers are driven from their towns. Then Christianity shall have come here to the land. The descendants of the former rulers are dishonored and brought to misery; we are christianized, while they treat us like animals.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. XI; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Great Deluge Again: The Descent over Jehoshaphat
title.zh: 大洪水再臨：於約沙法谷降臨

texts.period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c.; Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. X

texts.license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: When the law of the katun shall have run its course, God will bring about a great deluge again which will be the end of the world. When this is over, the Lord Jesus Christ shall descend on a great cloud over the valley of Jehoshaphat beside Jerusalem, to level off the world for the good and the bad, the conquerors and the captives.
summary.zh: 卡特倫之法運行既畢，上帝必再降大洪水，以為世界之終。洪荒既過，主耶穌基督將乘大雲降於耶路撒冷旁約沙法谷之上，為善人與惡人、征服者與被俘者，夷平世界。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: But when the law of the katun shall have run its course, then God will bring about a great deluge again which will be the end of the world. When this is over, then our Lord Jesus Christ shall descend over the valley of Jehoshaphat beside the town of Jerusalem where he redeemed us with his holy blood.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. X; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: He shall descend on a great cloud to bear true testimony that he was once obliged to suffer, stretched out on a cross of wood. Then shall descend in his great power and glory the true God who created heaven and earth and everything on earth. He shall descend to level off the world for the good and the bad, the conquerors and the captives.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. X; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Language of Zuyua: The Interrogation of the Chiefs

region.en: Zuyua (mythic place of power), Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 祖尤瓦（神權之地），墨西哥猶加敦

texts.period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c.; Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. IX

texts.license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: The first head-chief interrogates the chieftains in the Language of Zuyua — a riddle-speech that only the lineage learned may answer. 'Bring me the firefly of the night' means a smoking tube of tobacco; 'the beckoning tongue of the jaguar' is fire; 'your daughter, pale of face' is a calabash of atole; 'the winged jaguar' is a horse with bells and a red-thread crest. Those who know are cheerful; the ignorant shall be sad and lose their seats.
summary.zh: 第一酋首以祖尤瓦之語審問諸酋——此謎語之言，唯受教於族系者能答。「夜之螢火蟲」意指煙管中的菸草；「 jaguar 的招引之舌」是火；「面容蒼白的妳的女兒」是一碗阿托莱玉米糊；「有翼的 jaguar」是繫鈴戴紅線冠的馬。知者喜悅，不知者憂愁而失其位。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: 'Son, bring me the firefly of the night. Its odor shall pass to the north and to the west. Bring with it the beckoning tongue of the jaguar.' 'It is well, father.' What he asks for is a smoking tube filled with tobacco. The beckoning tongue of the jaguar for which he asks is fire.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. IX; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: 'Son, bring me your daughter that I may see her. Pale is her face and very beautiful. White are her head-covering and her sash.' What he asks for is a white calabash cup filled with atole. 'Son, bring me a woman with a very white and well rounded calf.' He wants a jicama: tucking back the skirt is peeling the skin. 'Bring me a very beautiful woman with a very white countenance; I will cast down her skirt and her loose dress before me.' This is a turkey-hen for him to eat; casting down her skirt means plucking its feathers.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. IX; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then our lord, the first head-chief, calls the chiefs: 'If you are head-chiefs here in the land, go and get the winged jaguar, and come and give it to me to eat. Put his bead collar on him properly, put on his crest properly.' Those who are ignorant shall be sad at heart and say nothing. This jaguar for which he asks is the chief's horse which he wishes to eat: the bead collar is its little bells; the crest is a red thread; it is to be completely saddled and bridled. The language of Zuyua.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. IX; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Mounds the Great Men Built

texts.period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c.; Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. IV

texts.license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: The history of how the mounds came to be constructed by the heathen: for three score and fifteen katuns they were constructed by the great men, thirteen katuns and six years in all — fifteen four-hundreds of scores of mounds and fifty more, all over the land, from the sea to the base of the land, with names for them and for the wells.
summary.zh: 記異教徒如何築丘：丘由偉人們築造，歷三又十五卡特倫，共十三卡特倫又六年——丘之總數十五個四百之計又五十，遍布全地，自海至地之基，丘與井皆有名字。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: The history which I have written of how the mounds came to be constructed by the heathen. During three score and fifteen katuns they were constructed. The great men made them. On this day I have written how the great mounds came to be built by the lineages and all the things which the rulers did; they were the ones who built the mounds.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. IV; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: It took thirteen katuns and six years for them to construct them. Fifteen four-hundreds were the scores of their mounds, and fifty more made the total count of the mounds they constructed all over the land. From the sea to the base of the land they created names for them as well as for the wells.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. IV; not verbatim throughout.

region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦埃卡布港

texts.period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c.; Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. V

texts.license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: In Katun 11 Ahau the foreigners seized the port of Ecab, coming from the east. They were the first to eat the pond-apple for breakfast, and so they were named: the foreigners who ate pond-apples, the foreigners who sucked pond-apples. Nacom Balam, the householder they seized at Ecab, was the first to be taken by the first captain, Don Juan de Montejo.
summary.zh: 十一阿赫卡特倫之際，異邦人自東方而來，奪取埃卡布港。他們是最早以番荔枝為早餐的人，因此得名：食番荔枝的異邦人、吸食番荔枝的異邦人。他們在埃卡布擒獲的屋主納科姆·巴拉姆，是首位被初代隊長胡安·德·蒙特霍擒獲的人。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: A record of the katuns and years when the Province of Yucatan was first seized by the foreigners, the white men. It was, they say, in Katun 11 Ahau that they seized the port of Ecab. They came from the east when they arrived. They say they were the first to eat the pond-apple for breakfast; this was the reason they called them the foreigners who ate pond-apples, foreigners who sucked pond-apples.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. V; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: This is the name of the householder whom they seized at Ecab: Nacom Balam was his name. He was the first to be seized at Ecab by the first Spanish captain, Don Juan de Montejo, the first conqueror. It was still the same katun when they arrived at Ichcaanziho. After the Itza were dispersed, it was fifteen score years when the foreigners arrived.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. V; not verbatim throughout.

title.en: The Katun of the Plumeria Flower: Submit or Be Uprooted
title.zh: 雞蛋花卡特倫：順服或被連根拔起

texts.period: Chumayel MS. written late 18th c.; Roys translation 1933

source.work: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel, trans. Ralph L. Roys, 1933, ch. XV

texts.license: Public domain (Roys 1933, not renewed at US Copyright Office)

summary.en: In the katun of the Plumeria flower comes the forceful one: head like a jaguar, long of tooth, body withered, heart pierced with sorrow — his speech false and mad. Chilam Balam counsels submission to the unhappy destiny of the katun: refuse, and you shall be moved from where your feet are rooted, gnaw the trunks of trees, and die as the deer die, going forth from your settlement.
summary.zh: 雞蛋花卡特倫之際，強橫者將至：首如 jaguar，齒長身枯，心如刀割——其言偽而狂。奇拉姆·巴拉姆勸眾順服卡特倫之厄運：若不順服，必被從立足之處連根拔起，啃食樹幹草莖，如鹿之死，倉皇離去。

sensitivity.note: Published colonial-era text; quote/paraphrase of Roys public-domain translation only.

passages.text: Then there shall be present the forceful one, there would be Nine Mountains, Yuma-une-tziuit, the quetzal, the green bird. No one understands the penance among the rulers in the twelfth tun when he declared his name. Like a jaguar is his head, long is his tooth, withered is his body, like a dog is his body. His heart is pierced with sorrow. Sweet is his food, sweet is his drink.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. XV; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Give yourselves up, my younger brothers, my older brothers, submit to the unhappy destiny of the katun which is to come. If you do not submit, you shall be moved from where your feet are rooted. If you do not submit, you shall gnaw the trunks of trees and herbs. If you do not submit, it shall be as when the deer die, so that they go forth from your settlement.
passages.note: Quoted from Roys translation (1933), ch. XV; lightly condensed; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Then even when the ruler himself goes forth, he shall return within your settlement bearing nothing. There shall come such a pestilence that the vultures enter the houses, a time of great death among the wild animals. There shall be three kinds of bread: the bread-nut shall be their bread in the katun of the Plumeria flower.
passages.note: Condensed from Roys translation (1933), ch. XV; not verbatim throughout.
